lab_title: Apparent Retrograde Motion: Solving the Planetary Puzzle
top_level_objectives: Explain the observational phenomenon of apparent retrograde motion from Earth's perspective.
Describe how the geocentric model accounted for retrograde motion using epicycles.
Demonstrate how the heliocentric model explains retrograde motion as an optical illusion caused by relative orbital speeds.
Analyze how a planet's distance from the Sun affects the scale and duration of its retrograde motion.

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the phenomenon of retrograde motion from an observer's perspective on Earth's surface.
key_visuals: A semi-dome of the night sky (planetarium style) showing constellations like Taurus and Gemini.
A glowing path representing Mars's movement across the sky over several months, featuring a distinct loop where it slows, reverses direction, and loops back.
A time-scrubbing interface showing the passing of calendar months and days.
student_actions: Use a virtual time scrubber to advance the calendar, watching Mars drift eastward, slow down, loop westward (retrograde), and resume its eastward path.
Tap on specific dates along Mars's path to read descriptions of how ancient astronomers documented this perplexing behavior.

scenes.brief_purpose: Explore the complex geocentric solution (Ptolemaic model) that used epicycles to explain this apparent reversal.
key_visuals: A geocentric 3D model centered on a stationary Earth.
Mars orbiting on a small circular path (epicycle), which itself orbits Earth on a larger circular path (deferent).
A dynamic projection line showing how the combined circular motions project a looping path onto a distant star sphere.
student_actions: Turn a physical-style crank to rotate the model, observing how Mars's combination of two circular paths creates a looping visual path from Earth's center.
Toggle on/off the projection line to see how hard Ptolemy had to work to make the geometry fit actual observations.

scenes.brief_purpose: Shift to a heliocentric perspective to observe the true physical motion of Earth and Mars orbiting the Sun.
key_visuals: A top-down, interactive 3D solar system model featuring a central glowing Sun, Earth on a fast inner orbit, and Mars on a slower outer orbit.
Orbital speed vectors (arrows) indicating that Earth travels faster than Mars.
student_actions: Pinch and zoom to inspect the relative orbital speeds of Earth and Mars.
Press a 'Play/Pause' button to watch Earth catch up to and pass the slower-moving Mars in their respective circular orbits.

scenes.brief_purpose: Deconstruct the 'overtaking' mechanism to show how relative motion projects the apparent retrograde loop.
key_visuals: The 3D heliocentric model from Scene 3, but with dynamic sightline beams projecting from Earth, through Mars, onto a distant cylindrical star screen.
Numbered markers (1 through 5) along Earth's and Mars's orbits, corresponding to matching numbered stars/positions on the background screen.
student_actions: Step the simulation frame-by-frame through the overtaking phase (positions 1-5).
Observe how the line of sight drifts eastward, reverses westward when Earth passes Mars, and then returns to eastward motion, demonstrating that the 'loop' is an optical illusion of relative motion.
Interact with a mini 'car passing' analogy visual to reinforce how a slower car next to you appears to move backward when you overtake it.

scenes.brief_purpose: Compare Mars's retrograde motion with that of more distant outer planets like Jupiter and Saturn.
key_visuals: An expanded heliocentric model showing Earth, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.
A split-screen comparison interface showing the retrograde loops of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn side-by-side on the star dome.
student_actions: Select Jupiter or Saturn to view their respective orbital paths and speeds relative to Earth.
Run the simulation to see how Earth overtakes these distant giants, noting that because they are much farther away, their apparent loops are smaller and tighter.
Complete an interactive sorting activity matching the size of the retrograde loop to the planet's distance from Earth.

scenes.brief_purpose: Synthesize and assess the student's understanding of retrograde motion and its historical role in astronomical models.
key_visuals: An interactive assessment space featuring a simplified heliocentric diagram on one side and an empty star path on the other.
student_actions: Drag and drop Earth into the correct position on its orbit (relative to Mars) that corresponds to the peak of the retrograde loop (opposition).
Answer multiple-choice questions explaining why the heliocentric model is preferred (Occam's razor, simplicity, natural explanation of retrograde motion) over the geocentric model.
